clue.text: Trouble began under sea … or lower?

definitions.note: read as one that lows, i.e. a creature that moos; the question mark flags the odd reading

indicators.note: trouble as a verb means to disturb or stir up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Something started going wrong beneath the waves, or perhaps further down still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' looks like the comparative of low, but it is the noun 'one that lows': a cow or bull.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scottish beef breed of cattle moos, so it is literally something that lows.

clue.text: Narrow-minded and maybe retired?

indicators.note: the question mark asks the solver to read retired as put to bed, the linker inside the bed

parts.note: to have retired for the night is to have gone to bed
the word 'and' is an example of a linker, a joining word

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of being intolerant and perhaps no longer working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is not a link word here: it is the thing described, a linker. 'retired' puts it to bed, inside BED, with the question mark flagging the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse with blinkers sees only straight ahead, so a person so described has a restricted outlook.

clue.text: Attacks are loud on a Tory leader, initially

indicators.note: said out loud, so the word are is taken for the letter it sounds like

parts.note: the word are is pronounced like the letter R
Iain Duncan Smith, a former Conservative leader, is known by his initials

explanation.surface: A political row: noisy assaults on a Conservative leader in their early days.
explanation.walkthrough: IDS is Iain Duncan Smith, Conservative Party leader 2001-03, routinely called by his initials in the British press.
explanation.definitionFit: Raids are sudden assaults or incursions, so attacks is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Most impressive! Let's reread communication

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its last letter is kept

parts.note: something epic is grand and impressive

indicators.note: to reread here is to read the letters in a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation of admiration, then an invitation to read something again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most' trims EPIC to EPI; 'reread' rearranges LETS into STLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter, especially a formal one like those of the New Testament apostles, is a written communication.

clue.text: Fledgling gets encouraged to climb, having something to fall back on

indicators.note: to climb says the hidden letters are read backwards
the fodder words are said to have, or contain, the letters wanted

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A young bird is urged to go upwards, with a safety net behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition included 'having', but the answer is a noun, so 'having' is the hidden signal (the words have it) and the definition is 'something to fall back on'. In a down clue, 'to climb' reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Savings put aside are a reserve one can rely on if things go wrong.

clue.text: Charlie no longer operating, welcomes doctors into country

indicators.note: a word that welcomes others takes them inside itself

parts.note: null means void or no longer in force

indicators.note: into says the doctors go inside the country

parts.note: UK is the United Kingdom
MB is a Bachelor of Medicine, so MBS are doctors

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie has stopped practising and invites physicians into the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name, but in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a charlie is a silly person, a dimwit or idiot.

clue.text: Part of Oxford University course, right?

parts.note: PPE, Philosophy, Politics and Economics, is a famous Oxford degree course

explanation.surface: A query about whether some element of an Oxford degree is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' looks like the university, but here it is an Oxford shoe, a laced leather shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: The top section of a shoe, above the sole, is its upper, and an Oxford is a type of shoe.

clue.text: Worth a trial?

parts.note: read 'a trial' as a pest or irritation and 'worth' as its value

explanation.surface: Is this case worth taking to court, or this idea worth testing?
explanation.walkthrough: 'trial' suggests a court case or test, but it means a trying, annoying thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the usefulness of being troublesome, such as leverage gained by being an irritant.

clue.text: PM that is prepared to spin, getting credit

parts.note: Gordon Brown was UK Prime Minister 2007-10
IE (id est) means that is

indicators.note: letters prepared are made ready in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A prime minister ready to put a spin on things, and being praised for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared to spin' reads as willing to give a political spin, but 'prepared' rearranges TO SPIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Notional merit earned by pleasing someone, especially a superior, is a form of credit.

clue.text: Twice I let suit run public services

indicators.note: run as in a stocking that has run, its threads pulled out of order
twice means the single letter is written two times

explanation.surface: Someone has twice allowed a lawsuit to go ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas, water and electricity supply companies provide public services and are called by this name.

clue.text: Little time for a gloomy type

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a short time
per means for each or for a, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: A short wait before someone miserable turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: One who mopes is sulky and miserable, a gloomy kind of person.

clue.text: Nancy's lover is 21 on film

indicators.note: the 21 across answer means a turn to face the opposite way, so the word is is turned round

parts.note: Kes is the 1969 Ken Loach film about a boy and his kestrel

explanation.surface: A woman's boyfriend appears in a movie, doing what 21 across says.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Sikes is Nancy's brutal lover in Dickens's Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Oliver Twist, the burglar Bill is the man Nancy loves and who murders her.

clue.text: Mammal disconcerted eating Welshman

indicators.note: a word eating another holds it inside

parts.note: to throw someone is to disconcert them, so threw means disconcerted
Rees is a common Welsh name

explanation.surface: An animal is unsettled while devouring a man from Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disconcerted' looks like an anagram signal, but it is a synonym, the past tense of throw in its sense of unsettle.
explanation.definitionFit: This small squirrel-like insectivore of South-East Asia is a mammal.

clue.text: Was a candidate returned? Consider recount

indicators.note: returned means the word is sent back the way it came

parts.note: to run in an election is to be a candidate, so ran
to rate something is to consider or judge it

explanation.surface: An election query: was the candidate re-elected, and should there be a recount?
explanation.walkthrough: 'recount' suggests counting votes again; it is to tell a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount events is to tell or relate them, a straight synonym.

clue.text: One relative without uniform, another without clothes

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the relative goes round

parts.note: an aunt is a relative
one is A, the indefinite article
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
another relative, abbreviated REL

explanation.surface: One family member lacks a uniform; another has no clothes on at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' first means outside: AUNT round A gives AUNAT. 'another' then stands for another relative, abbreviated REL.
explanation.definitionFit: French for in the natural state, used in English to mean naked.

clue.text: 'Fish good for us' (Nancy's friend)

parts.note: what is for us is ours, so our
Nancy is a French city, and the French for friend is ami

explanation.surface: A slogan claims fish is healthy, attributed to Nancy's pal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nancy' here is the city in north-eastern France, not the woman of 12 across.
explanation.definitionFit: This freshwater fish of Asia is popular in aquariums.

clue.text: Fabulous body — one quietly captivated for starters

indicators.note: a word that has captivated others holds them inside
the body of a word is what remains without its extremities

parts.note: fabulous and fantastic are synonyms
one is the Roman numeral I
P (piano) is the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A wonderful physique has charmed someone without fuss, at least at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' strips FANTASTIC of its ends to ANTASTI, which holds IP. 'for starters' looks like 'initially' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian appetisers served before the main meal are starters.

clue.text: Finishes posting, having succeeded at last

indicators.note: at last says the letter is moved to the very end

parts.note: posting a letter is sending it
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: Someone stops sending messages once they have finally achieved what they wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: SENDING has its S moved to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The conclusions or final parts of things are their finishes.

clue.text: Prospect of the drink running out — wives each getting stuck in

indicators.note: the abbreviation for each is pushed inside the other letters
wives running out scatter, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: No more booze, as wives dash off and each one tucks in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running out' rearranges the wives into S VIEW. 'the drink' is crossword slang for the sea, so the definition runs to four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A view of the sea, 'the drink', is a prospect, an outlook over it.

clue.text: Part company after rent increase

parts.note: rent as the past tense of rend means torn or split
to up something is to increase it

explanation.surface: A couple separate after the landlord raises the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like money paid to a landlord; it means torn.
explanation.definitionFit: To separate, especially as a couple ending a relationship, is to part company.

clue.text: Make more agreeable to repeatedly small number

parts.note: small is given twice, first as S, the abbreviation, then as wee, Scottish for small
ten is a number

explanation.surface: Instructions to keep making a tiny figure more pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweeten a deal or a person is to make them more pleasing or palatable.

clue.text: 'Answer attack with force' (one in US military command)

parts.note: a bout is a fit or attack, as of illness
F is the physics symbol for force
an ace is a one in cards

explanation.surface: A motto urging forceful retaliation, issued by a single officer in the American army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attack' looks like an assault, but here it is a bout, as of fever.
explanation.definitionFit: The American drill order to turn round 180 degrees; the British form is about turn.

clue.text: Better be enough — dismissed previously

indicators.note: previously says the dismissed part comes before the other

parts.note: a batter dismissed in cricket is out
to do is to suffice, as in 'that will do'

explanation.surface: Something had better be sufficient, having been rejected before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is a verb: to surpass.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass or beat someone is to better them, a verb sense.

clue.text: About to have almost a month on island

parts.note: C (circa) means about

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short of the end

parts.note: April is a month

explanation.surface: Someone is about to spend most of a month on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'nearly' but is C, circa.
explanation.definitionFit: The island in the Bay of Naples is a famous holiday resort.

clue.text: Grossly stupid councillor Trump's behind

parts.note: Trump points to American usage, where the backside is the ass

explanation.surface: A local politician sits behind Donald Trump, who is called very dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' is the US president's name standing for American English.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass describes gross stupidity or insensitivity, a dictionary sense.

clue.text: Brute's associates in dramatic murder back on run, say

indicators.note: back means the words are turned round

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar the dying Caesar says 'Et tu, Brute?', so the words keeping company with Brute are et tu
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Brutus's accomplices in a stage killing are back on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ET TU into UTTE; 'say' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak or voice words is to say them aloud, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Travelling by rail, I missed getting seat

indicators.note: missed means the letter is left out

parts.note: travelling by rail is going in train
to seat someone is to make them sit

explanation.surface: A rail traveller complains about not getting a seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missed' removes the second I from IN TRAIN, giving INTRAN; 'getting' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods or people on the way between places are on the move, travelling.

clue.text: Copying the example of fans at match

parts.note: a following is a body of fans
to suit is to match, as colours do

explanation.surface: Supporters at a football match imitate each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' looks like the game the fans attend; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games, playing the led suit; figuratively it means doing as others did.
